additions.reason: Line 2 opens with 'וְזֶהוּ' — the standard Likutey Moharan formula for introducing a Rabbinic or scriptural text as the bechina-expression of the preceding statement. The Rebbe is saying: THIS (= the Mishnah's formula) IS that [= what I just described in line 1]. The phenomenon described in line 1 — clinging (דְּבֵקוּת) to Torah words from the Tzaddik — IS the same essential act as 'benefiting from (הַנֶּהֱנֶה מִ) words of Torah' in the Mishnah. The two phrases name the same spiritual reality from different angles: line 1 emphasizes the source (the Tzaddik's mouth) and the mode (דְּבֵקוּת, attachment); the Mishnah emphasizes the experiential result of the act (הֲנָאָה, pleasure/benefit). They are parallel aspects — the Rebbe does not say one CAUSES the other; he says one IS the other ('וְזֶהוּ'). This is a bechina equivalence, not a causal connection.

additions.reason: The Rebbe's re-reading of the Mishnah's second clause ('נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם') establishes a bechina-equivalence with the state described in line 1: clinging to Torah from the Tzaddik IS the state of having one's life taken out of / elevated beyond this world. This is not a causal claim (Torah-attachment does not PRODUCE world-transcendence as its separate effect — they are simultaneous co-descriptions of the same elevated state). The Rebbe frames this with amazement ('תָּמֵהַּ אֲנִי, אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר') — expressing that to cling to Torah from the Tzaddik IS to already be in a state where worldly life cannot be tolerated or desired. The 'אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר' (how is it possible) formulation is not causal but descriptive of co-presence: the person who is in state A (Torah-attachment) is simultaneously in state B (world-transcendence), and state B IS the meaning of 'נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם.' The Rebbe reads the Mishnah's 'נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם' positively — his life-force is drawn up and out of the world into the divine — not as a privation (losing one's life) but as elevation (life transcends the world). This is the core hermeneutical move of the Torah.

analysis_notes.hermeneutical_note: Torah #157's key interpretive move is the re-reading of the Mishnah's 'נוֹטֵל חַיָּיו מִן הָעוֹלָם.' The standard reading of Avot 4:1 (according to most commentators) is either (a) 'removes himself from the world' — i.e., neglects worldly needs and thus harms himself, or (b) 'takes his life/sustenance from the world through Torah.' Rebbe Nachman applies a third reading: 'his life/vitality is elevated and taken out of the world by Torah' — i.e., his nefesh rises beyond worldly consciousness and worldly desires can no longer take hold of him. This elevation-reading is what the 'וְהָבֵן הֵיטֵב' (understand this well) at the end of the Torah signals — the apparent meaning is not the deep meaning. The deep meaning is that Torah-attachment from the Tzaddik generates a state of spiritual elevation so profound that the earthly dimension of human existence loses its experiential grip. This is a classic Hasidic re-reading that turns a potentially negative Mishnaic statement into a description of the highest spiritual state.
